title: Moraxella, Kingella, and Other Gram-Negative Cocci

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man presented with a 1-week history of cough, pleuritic chest pain, and low-grade fevers. He was known to have chronic obstructive pulmonary disorder and had a smoking pack year history of 60 years. Investigations: CXR revealed a dense infiltrate in the right lower lobe Sputum microscopy revealed numerous gram-negative cocci, many in pairs
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate therapy?
questions.explanation: Amoxicillin/clavulanate In addition to Haemophilus influenzae and Streptococcus pneumoniae, Moraxella catarrhalis is a common cause of exacerbations of COPD. The Gram stain depicts gramnegative cocci in pairs, typical of Moraxella catarrhalis. The best answer choice would be amoxicillin/clavulanate due to increasing resistance noted to TMP–SMX and tetracyclines for Moraxella. Amoxicillin/clavulanate would be preferred over a quinolone.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q6

questions.question: Match each congenital finding to the congenital infection with which it is classically associated.

parts.text: Osteitis
Periventricular calcifications
Scarring
Heart failure
Cataracts

parts_raw.text: A.  Osteitis
B.  Periventricular calcifications
C.  Scarring
D.  Heart failure
E.  Cataracts

questions.model_answer: a) Osteitis (osteochondritis, periostitis, "Wimberger sign"): congenital syphilis (Treponema pallidum). b) Periventricular (periventricular/subependymal) calcifications: congenital cytomegalovirus (CMV). c) Cicatricial scarring (dermatomal skin scarring, limb hypoplasia): congenital varicella syndrome (VZV). d) Heart failure/hydrops from myocarditis or severe anemia: parvovirus B19 (also myocarditis in rubella, syphilis, and Chagas disease). e) Cataracts (with microphthalmia, plus PDA/pulmonic stenosis, sensorineural deafness): congenital rubella syndrome.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only cataracts (rubella) is grounded in this chapter (Table 152.1, p. 2009); the osteitis-syphilis, periventricular calcification-CMV, scarring-VZV, and heart-failure-parvovirus B19 associations are standard TORCH teaching from the respective Mandell chapters, not this one.

cohort_answer.text:
Syphilis
CMV
Varicella
Parvovirus B19/rubella/syphilis/Chagas (myocarditis)
Rubella

questions.question: Syphilitic aortitis is suspected in a patient with a positive CMIA, TPPA, and FTA-ABS but a negative RPR.
questions.question_raw: 14.  Syphilis aortitis suspected with positive CMIA, TPPA, FTA-ABs but negative RPR.

parts.text: Explain the serologies in the context of aortitis.
What treatment is indicated? Give drug, route, and frequency or duration.
What other test is indicated?

parts_raw.text: A.  Explain the serologies in the context of aortitis.
B.  What treatment is indicated, give drug, route and frequency or duration?
C.  What other test is indicated?

questions.model_answer:
a) The positive treponemal tests (CMIA, TPPA, FTA-ABS) confirm treponemal infection and remain reactive for life in ~85% of patients regardless of treatment; the negative nontreponemal test (RPR) reflects the fact that RPR titres frequently decline and may serorevert to negative in untreated late/tertiary disease. The pattern (reactive treponemal + non-reactive RPR) is therefore fully compatible with late/tertiary (cardiovascular) syphilis causing aortitis, and a negative RPR does NOT exclude it.
b) Cardiovascular (tertiary, non-neurological) syphilis: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM once weekly x 3 doses (total 7.2 million units).
c) Lumbar puncture for CSF examination to exclude concurrent neurosyphilis (its presence mandates a neurosyphilis IV penicillin regimen instead).
questions.beyond_mandell: Serologic interpretation and cardiovascular-syphilis regimen per CDC 2021 STI Treatment Guidelines / PHAC Canadian STI Guidelines and Mandell syphilis chapter.

cohort_answer.text:
Tertiary syphilis
Benzathine Penicillin G 2.4million units IM weekly x 3 doses (assuming no CNS involvement)
Lumbar puncture

questions.question: Congenital syphilis management scenarios.

parts.text: The baby is asymptomatic. The mother was treated at 37 weeks with a single dose of IM penicillin. What do you do?
The mother was treated early with IM penicillin x3; her RPR fell from 1:64 to 1:2, and the baby's RPR is 1:2. What do you do?
The mother was treated early with her RPR falling from 1:32 to 1:2, and the baby's RPR is undetectable. What do you do?

parts_raw.text: Baby is asymptomatic. Mom treated at 37wks IM pen x1. What do you do?
Mom treated early IM pen x3. RPR 1:64 dropped to 1:2. Baby RPR 1:2. What do you do?
Mom treated early 1:32 to 1:2, baby undetectable. What do you do?

questions.model_answer:
a) Maternal treatment is INADEQUATE: penicillin was given <4 weeks before delivery (and a single dose is inadequate for latent disease). Perform a full infant evaluation (CBC with platelets, CSF for VDRL/cell count/protein, long-bone radiographs, and clinical exam) and treat the infant for congenital syphilis with aqueous crystalline penicillin G 50,000 U/kg IV q12h (first 7 days) then q8h for a 10-day course.
b) Maternal treatment was adequate and early with an appropriate (>=4-fold) serologic response, and the infant RPR is not >=4-fold the maternal titre. Infant is low risk: give a single dose of benzathine penicillin G 50,000 U/kg IM with close serologic follow-up.
c) Adequately/early-treated mother with an appropriate response and a non-reactive infant RPR: lowest-risk infant. No treatment required beyond routine clinical and serologic follow-up (a single dose of benzathine penicillin G 50,000 U/kg IM is an accepted option if follow-up cannot be ensured).
questions.beyond_mandell: Risk stratification and infant regimens per CDC 2021 STI Treatment Guidelines / AAP Red Book congenital syphilis algorithm.

cohort_answer.text:
Treat baby for congenital syphilis (must be treated >4weeks before delivery)
No need treatment
[answer not documented]

questions.question: A patient with syphilis is treated with a beta-lactam and develops the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction.
questions.question_raw: Patient with syphilis treated with a beta-lactam. Develops Jarisch-Herxheimer syndrome.

parts.text: Which stage carries the highest risk of the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction?
List 3 clinical manifestations of syphilis in which the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction would cause serious complications.

parts_raw.text: What stage is highest risk for Jarisch-Herxheimer syndrome?
List 3 clinical manifestations of syphilis that would result in complications if J-H developed.

questions.model_answer:
a) Secondary syphilis (highest spirochaete burden), carrying the greatest risk of the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction.
b) (1) Neurosyphilis (worsening cerebral/meningeal inflammation, seizures). (2) Ocular syphilis (inflammatory worsening threatening vision). (3) Cardiovascular syphilis / aortitis (risk of coronary ostial occlusion or aortic aneurysm rupture; note also pregnancy, where it can precipitate preterm labour and fetal distress).
questions.beyond_mandell: Jarisch-Herxheimer risk sites per CDC 2021 STI Treatment Guidelines and Mandell syphilis chapter.

cohort_answer.text: Secondary stage is highest risk. || Manifestations: Ocular; Neurosyphilis; Cardiovascular (sudden death from coronary occlusion/aneurysm rupture); ?Pregnancy.

questions.question: A patient presents with multiple anal ulcers.

parts.text: Name two possible organisms causing this.

parts_raw.text: Name 2 possible organisms causing this.

questions.model_answer: (1) Herpes simplex virus (HSV-2 or HSV-1) — anal and perianal infection is common in sexually active MSM, and herpes is the predominant cause of genital/anogenital ulcers worldwide; (2) Treponema pallidum. Detection of HSV does not exclude coinfection with T. pallidum or Haemophilus ducreyi, which should be considered in the appropriate epidemiologic context.

questions.question: A 40-year-old HIV-positive man has a positive EIA for Treponema pallidum. He was never previously screened or treated for syphilis. Two years ago he had an anaphylactic reaction to cefixime given for gonorrhea.
questions.question_raw: 13. 40-year old HIV + patient has a positive EIA for T. pallidum. He was never screened prior to now, and never received treatment for syphilis. He had an anaphylactic reaction to cefixime 2 years ago when treated for gonorrhea.

parts.text: List 3 possible indications for a lumbar puncture in this patient.
List 3 tests you would request on the cerebrospinal fluid.
He is diagnosed with neurosyphilis. Name 2 important elements of your antimicrobial therapeutic approach for this patient (be precise about dose, duration, etc.).
List 2 laboratory criteria that would indicate failure of your treatment.

parts_raw.text: List 3 possible indications for a lumbar puncture in this patient
c) List 3 tests you would ask for on cerebrospinal fluid.
d) He is diagnosed with neurosyphilis. Name 2 important elements of your antimicrobial therapeutic approach for this patient (be precise – dose, duration, etc.)
e) List 2 laboratory criteria that would indicate a failure of your treatment

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Neurologic, ophthalmic, or otologic signs/symptoms. (2) Evidence of active tertiary disease (e.g., aortitis, gumma) or serologic treatment failure. (3) HIV co-infection with high-risk features (serum RPR >=1:32 and/or CD4 <350 cells/uL).
b) (1) CSF-VDRL. (2) CSF white cell count with differential. (3) CSF protein.
c) (1) Because of the prior beta-lactam (cephalosporin) anaphylaxis, perform penicillin allergy skin testing and desensitize, since penicillin is the preferred and best-evidenced neurosyphilis agent. (2) Aqueous crystalline penicillin G 18-24 million units/day IV, given as 3-4 million units q4h (or continuous infusion), for 10-14 days.
d) (1) CSF-VDRL titre fails to decline 4-fold (or rises) by 6-12 months. (2) CSF WBC fails to normalize by 6 months (persistent pleocytosis); accompanied by failure of the serum RPR to fall 4-fold.
questions.beyond_mandell: LP indications, CSF testing, neurosyphilis regimen, and failure criteria per CDC 2021 STI Treatment Guidelines / PHAC Canadian STI Guidelines.

cohort_answer.text: Canadian STI guidelines indications for LP: Presence of neurologic or ophthalmic symptoms/signs; Congenital syphilis; Previously treated patients who fail to achieve adequate serologic response; Tertiary syphilis; HIV patients with neurologic symptoms/signs; Late latent syphilis; RPR≥1:32 dilutions, CD4<350 or treated syphilis with suboptimal decline in VDRL/RPR titre. Some experts recommend CSF exam in all HIV-infected individuals and all patients with RPR≥1:32. CSF tests: VDRL (most specific); Cell count with differential; Protein. Treatment: skin test for penicillin -> if negative treat with penicillin, if positive consider desensitization then treat with penicillin (less data on CTX efficacy for neurosyphilis). Regimens: Aqueous crystalline penicillin G IV 3-4 million units q4hr x10-14d; Ceftriaxone 2g IV/IM q24hr x10-14d. Failure criteria: CSF VDRL rising 2 dilutions or more; CSF WBC fails to resolve (usually first to improve). Other criteria: clinical progression; at 2yr post-treatment still persistently abnormal CSF WBC or VDRL positive; persistently low CSF VDRL titre.

questions.question: A patient adequately treated for syphilis two years ago now has a negative RPR and a positive treponemal test, and still has ongoing risk factors.
questions.question_raw: You see a patient who has been treated adequately for syphilis two years ago. He has a negative RPR and a positive treponemal test. He still has risk factors.

parts.text: Name 4 reasons why the treponemal test may be persistently positive.

parts_raw.text: Named 4 reason why the treponemal test may be persistent

questions.model_answer: (1) Past, adequately treated syphilis: treponemal antibodies persist for life in ~85% of patients regardless of therapy. (2) Reinfection given ongoing risk factors (treponemal tests remain positive; a new nontreponemal rise would be needed to confirm). (3) Untreated latent or tertiary syphilis elsewhere. (4) Cross-reacting endemic treponematoses (yaws, pinta, or bejel).
questions.beyond_mandell: Lifelong treponemal seroreactivity and cross-reactivity per CDC 2021 STI Treatment Guidelines and Mandell syphilis chapter.

cohort_answer.text: Treated syphilis; Early primary syphilis; Tertiary syphilis; Late latent syphilis; Endemic treponemal infection (not in this patient)

questions.question: A 2-year-old child presents with a few days of favouring the left leg due to right knee pain. Ultrasound is normal, but MRI shows bone marrow edema of the distal femur.
questions.question_raw: A 2-year old child presents with a few day history of favouring their left leg due to pain on the right knee. The child undergoes ultrasound showing no abnormality but an MRI shows bone marrow edema of the distal femur.

parts.text: What is the clinical diagnosis?
Blood cultures grow a gram-negative coccobacillus; what is the MOST likely organism?
What non-osteoarticular infection is this organism most likely to cause?

parts_raw.text: What is the clinical diagnosis?
The blood cultures result in a gram-negative coccobacilli, what is the MOST likely organism?
What NON-osteoarticular infection is this organism above most likely to cause?

questions.model_answer:
a) Osteomyelitis of the distal femur (acute osteoarticular infection).
b) Kingella kingae, the most common cause of osteoarticular infection in previously healthy children younger than 4 years, presenting subtly with often-normal acute-phase reactants.
c) Endocarditis (Kingella is the K of the HACEK group and, unlike its osteoarticular disease, can cause endocarditis at all ages, on native or prosthetic valves).

cohort_answer.text:
a) OM
b) Kingella kingae?
c) Endocarditis?

questions.question: Name 2 gram-negative bacteria that grow on blood and chocolate agar but not on MacConkey agar.

parts.text: 2 GNB that grow on blood and chocolate agar but not on MacConkey?

parts_raw.text: A) 2 GNB that grow on blood and chocolate agar but not on MAC?

questions.model_answer: (1) Haemophilus influenzae. (2) Aggregatibacter aphrophilus. Both are fastidious HACEK-group gram-negative organisms that require enriched media (X/V factors on chocolate agar) and do not grow on MacConkey. (Other acceptable different-genus answers: Eikenella corrodens, Pasteurella, Brucella, Francisella.)

cohort_answer.text: Actinobacillus, Gardnerella, Brucella, Francisella, Eikenella, Haemophilus, Campylobacter, Legionella, Bordetella, Helicobacter
